To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection is common in non‐transfused, HIV‐infected homosexual men, and that HCV RNA is detectable in about half of these individuals, even in the absence of serological markers of HCV infection.

hepatitis C virus infection is common in non‐intravenous‐drug‐using, nontransfused homosexual men, and that the presence of hepatitis C virus antibody is highly predictive of hepatitis C virus viraemia.

the prevalence of hepatitis c virus in nontransfuded, nonintravenous drug‐abusing male homosexual patients with human immunodeficency virus infection is several times that found in volunteer blood donors and that the hepatitis C virus infection does not appear to influence survival of patients with human immunodificency virus infection with or without manifestations AIDS.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following issues.
the epidemiology of hepatitis C virus and its relationship to human immunodeficiency (HIV) infection and survival in homosexual men.
the epidemiological and molecular aspects of HCV infection in the general population, in patients with HIV‐1 infection and in patients with chronic liver disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the hepatitis C virus is not a common cause of liver disease in homosexual men.

the prevalence of hepatitis B and hepatitis C is higher in HIV‐infexed patients than in HIV‐uninfected controls and that the prevalence of both viruses is higher in patients with HIV‐1 than those with HIV‐2.
the hepatitis C virus infection is a common infection in HIV infected homosexual men.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have demonstrated that hepatitis C virus infection in HIV‐infused patients is several times more frequent than in volunteer blood donor and that about half of patients sero‐ positive for hepatitis C antibody have detectable RNA.
hepatitis C is more common in HIV patients than in blood donors.
we were the first to describe the epidemiology of HCV in HIV infected patients.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hepatitis C virus is a common infection among HIV‐infected men, especially those without a history of intravenous drug use.
HIV‐infected individuals who do not use injection drugs are at risk of hepatitis C virus acquisition, and this is probably due to sexual transmission.
hepatitis C virus (HCV) is much more common among homosexual men with HIV than in the general population, and that it is not associated with an increased risk of death.
